extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, biologists, and scientifically-literate readers interested in variation and evolution
extracted.subtask_description: A set of general principles and observed regularities concerning variation, correlation of parts, reversion, and the action of natural and sexual selection on species and varieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of correlation of growth
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature of the bond of correlation is often obscure; certain malconformations frequently coexist and others rarely do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin gives many examples (blue eyes and deafness in cats; tortoise-shell colour with female sex; feathered feet and skin between toes in pigeons correlated with down on young birds; hair and teeth in the naked Turkish dog). Correlated structures may arise and modify important structures independently of utility and natural selection. These correlations can produce differences systematists consider important (e.g., in seeds and ovaries of ray vs central florets) without conferring obvious advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish correlation from inheritance
rubrics_metrics.description: Structures common to whole groups of species may be due to inheritance from an ancestor rather than to correlation of growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: two modifications in an ancient progenitor transmitted to a whole group could appear correlated though independent. Conversely, some apparent correlations across whole orders may result from limitations on how natural selection can act (e.g., winged seeds only occur in fruits which open, because selection for wings can act only there).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ray and central florets differences (correlation vs selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences between outer (ray) and inner (central) flowers in Compositae and Umbelliferae may result from correlated growth rather than direct adaptive advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences occur in corolla, seeds, and ovaries; some differences (seed shape) seem non-advantageous. Sprengel's idea that ray-florets attract insects is plausible and natural selection may act where advantageous, but many internal/external structural differences in florets likely arise from flow of nutriment or correlated development rather than selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of compensation (balancement of growth)
rubrics_metrics.description: The older law that increase of development on one side requires economising on the other ('in order to spend on one side, nature is forced to economise on the other side') holds to some extent, especially in domestic productions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: cattle giving much milk do not fatten readily; cabbage varieties do not yield both abundant foliage and oil-bearing seeds. Darwin cautions that it is hard to distinguish effects of direct natural selection from true withdrawal of nutriment causing compensation, and he doubts universal applicability in wild species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural selection economises by reducing superfluous structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural selection tends to reduce and save every part of the organisation when rendered superfluous, without necessarily causing a corresponding enlargement elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by parasitic cirripedes (e.g., Proteolepas) that lose shells/carapaces and large head segments when protected in host; the saving of developing unnecessary structures confers advantage and can be achieved gradually by selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variability of repeated parts (vegetative repetition)
rubrics_metrics.description: When any part or organ is repeated many times in the same individual (e.g., vertebrae, stamens), the number and structure of these repeated parts are more variable than parts occurring in smaller numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'vegetative repetition' may signal low organisation; parts performing diversified tasks are less specialized and thus more likely to vary. Multiple parts are also liable to variation in structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rudimentary parts are apt to be highly variable
rubrics_metrics.description: Rudimentary and aborted organs tend to be highly variable because their uselessness leaves them unchecked by natural selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such parts are subject to free play of growth laws, disuse effects, and tendency to reversion. Darwin notes variability of rudiments will be discussed further in later chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts extraordinarily developed within a species tend to be highly variable
rubrics_metrics.description: A part developed in any species in an extraordinary degree or manner, compared with the same part in allied species, tends to be highly variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cites Mr. Waterhouse and Professor Owen; applies strongly to secondary sexual characters and to recently and greatly modified structures (e.g., opercular valves in Pyrgoma barnacles). The rule applies only when the extraordinary development is unusual relative to closely allied species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recently accumulated modification correlates with higher variability
rubrics_metrics.description: If a part has undergone large and recent modification (since branching from a common progenitor), it will usually show greater variability until selection has fixed it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin explains that long-continued variability accumulated by selection can still leave 'generative variability' until selection and rejection have had time to make the new form constant; very old, widely shared modifications become as constant as other structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific characters are generally more variable than generic characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters that distinguish species from species (specific characters) tend to be more variable than characters common to a whole genus (generic characters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if some species in a genus have blue flowers and others red, flower colour is a specific character and may change between species; but if all species share blue flowers, variation in colour is a generic-level character and its variation is rarer. Darwin attributes this to inheritance from a common progenitor and the relative recency of change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary sexual characters are especially variable
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary sexual characters (characters attached to one sex but not directly to reproduction) are very variable and often differ more between closely allied species than do other parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin attributes this to sexual selection being less rigid than ordinary selection (it affects reproductive success rather than survival) and thus providing a wider scope for divergent change; such characters may also become sex-limited in expression during selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific and sexual differences tend to be displayed in same parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The secondary sexual differences between sexes of a species are often shown in the same parts of the organisation in which different species of the same genus differ from one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: tarsi joint number in Engidae varies among species and sexes; wing neuration in fossorial hymenoptera differs among species and sexes. Darwin explains this by descent from a variable progenitor and selection operating on the same variable parts for interspecific and sexual purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous variation and reversion among related forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinct species present analogous variations, and a variety of one species often assumes characters of an allied species or reverts to characters of an early progenitor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Domestic pigeons show analogous variations (e.g., reversed head feathers, feathered feet) across breeds likely inherited from a common parent. Reversion (atavism) may explain repeated appearance of ancestral characters; crossing breeds often reveals ancestral marks (e.g., rock-pigeon markings) suggesting inherited tendency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency to reversion can persist for many generations
rubrics_metrics.description: A tendency to reproduce a lost character may be inherited and can reappear after many generations, even if the direct genetic 'proportion of blood' from an ancestor is negligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin argues that reappearance is best explained by a persistent generative tendency each generation rather than sudden inheritance from a distant ancestor. He gives examples in pigeons and snapdragon (a rudiment of a fifth stamen frequently appears).

rubrics_metrics.name: Crossing related taxa can reveal ancestral characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Crosses between breeds or species may produce individuals showing characters intermediate between parents or resemblances to allied species (including ancestral traits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin notes many catalogued intermediate forms and gives examples in equids (stripes on asses, horses, mules, and quagga) where crossing or hybrid ancestry may reveal or amplify ancestral striping characters; such observations bear on distinguishing varieties from species.
